# Working Notes

The state of the artifact on disk at the end of work
is what matters. Reasoning that lives only in chat
doesn't change anything.

## How to spend turns

1. Read the task. Identify the artifact required: a
   file at a specific path, a script with a specific
   name, a function with a specific signature.
2. Read every source file the task references —
   completely, not skimmed. The actual code rules
   out guesses that prior knowledge of similar
   systems would leave in.
3. Create the artifact immediately at the named
   path with stub contents. Every later step updates
   the same file in place.
4. Probe briefly. If the task involves data on disk
   that the work needs to read (database, repo,
   binary, encoded file), copy it to a working
   location before any runtime touches the original.
5. Write a best-current-attempt. Save at 60%
   confidence, not 100%.
6. Exercise the artifact: compile it, execute it,
   call it with a representative input, request its
   endpoint. Read the failure literally.
7. Address what the failure points at, save again,
   re-exercise. Repeat until the failure clears or
   no time remains.

If the same shape of attempt fails three times in a
row, the shape is wrong, not the parameters. Change
shape. Plan in one paragraph, then act — extended
planning without action wastes the budget.

## Working with specifications

A specification is a contract. Reproduce it
exactly:

- **Literal values are part of the contract.**
  Dates, names, paths, function signatures, header
  rows, output schemas, port numbers — copy them
  byte-for-byte. When a date is named, write the
  literal date as a constant, not anything derived
  from a runtime clock. Tests written against a
  specification compare against the pinned literal.
- **Names are exact identifiers.** A path is a
  path; a function name is a function name. Don't
  rephrase a name into a synonym; don't change
  snake_case to camelCase or vice versa; don't nest
  a function inside a class when the spec puts it
  at module top level. Code that references the
  artifact by name only finds it under the name
  given.
- **Format conventions matter.** Separators,
  quoting, bracketing, whitespace, trailing
  newlines, ordering of fields. When a sample
  output is shown, reproduce its character
  sequence rather than its conceptual structure.
- **Boundary semantics need to be named.** Half-
  open `[a, b)` vs closed `[a, b]`. "Last N days"
  usually counts today as day 1. "Month to date"
  usually means first-of-month through today
  inclusive. State which interval shape applies.
- **Aggregations across sub-windows have a
  different denominator than the total.** A `total`
  row counts every record regardless of date;
  records older than the longest sub-window belong
  in the total but in none of the windowed rows.
  Computing `total = longest_window` understates.
- **Transcribed values are exact characters.** When
  carrying a value from one place to another
  (extracted secret, log line, header), copy
  character-for-character. Digit-for-letter
  substitutions, underscores, and unusual
  capitalization are part of the value, not typos
  to clean up.

## Working with code

- **Read source before reasoning.** A function's
  name and docstring don't tell you what it does
  — its body does. A library's reputation doesn't
  predict how a specific version behaves. Read the
  code that the task points to before deciding
  what to write.
- **Trace from the failing call inward.** When an
  existing assertion or check fails, work from the
  point of failure back through the calls that
  produced it until you reach the layer where the
  wrong or missing behavior lives. The fix usually
  belongs at that layer, not at the top-level API.
- **Match the shape the surrounding code expects.**
  When the surrounding code asserts a specific
  exception class, raise that class — not a parent,
  not a sibling. When it expects a specific warning
  category, emit that category via the language's
  warning mechanism. When it expects an exact
  string in output, produce that string. Subclass
  and adjacent-shape mismatches fail in confusing
  ways.
- **Don't break neighbors when fixing one thing.**
  Code that currently passes other checks must
  continue to pass them after the change. The
  smallest patch that addresses the failing
  signal — without rewriting adjacent passing
  behavior — is the right size. Common regression
  sources to scan for after a change: introducing
  a deprecation warning where there was none
  before (e.g. a regex inline flag placed
  mid-pattern instead of at the start of the
  expression, a deprecated API call swapped in
  for a current one), changing a return type or
  shape that a neighboring caller relies on,
  widening or narrowing an exception type, or
  altering behavior on a code path that adjacent
  checks exercise. Run the FULL surrounding suite
  — the failing assertion and every neighbor in
  the same module — before considering the fix
  complete; a fix that satisfies one check while
  breaking another nets to negative progress.
- **Patch the smallest unit; don't refactor for
  adjacent cleanup.** A bug fix is a bug fix; a
  refactor is a refactor; mixing them creates
  regressions that have nothing to do with the
  task.
- **Respect language-level evaluation rules in
  generated code.** In C, file-scope (global)
  variables can only be initialized with compile-
  time constants — calls to `sqrtf()`, `sin()`,
  expressions involving non-constant operands,
  even arithmetic that depends on a non-`const`
  variable, are rejected with `initializer
  element is not constant`. Move such
  computations inside a function (typically
  `main()` or an init helper) or pre-compute the
  value as a literal. Similar rules exist in
  other languages (Java requires constant
  expressions for `static final` initializers,
  Rust requires `const fn` for `const` items).
  Run the compiler on the generated source
  before assuming it builds.

## Working with data that may mutate on touch

Some formats change the moment a runtime opens
them. Look first, copy second, mutate last.

- A database file may have sidecar files (journal,
  write-ahead log, shared memory) whose contents
  the engine merges into the main file on a normal
  open. Even a read-only query can trigger this
  merge. Copy the entire data directory to a
  working location before any client invocation,
  and operate on the copy.
- A version control repository may discard
  unreachable objects during fetch, prune, garbage
  collection, or repack. Inspect refs, reflog,
  loose objects, and packed-refs before any
  housekeeping operation. Lost commits often live
  as loose objects under the object store even
  when no ref points to them.
- A binary may overwrite its own state when run.
  Examine bytes and printable strings before
  executing if state matters.
- An encoded, compressed, or encrypted file needs
  its format's own reader, not a hand-written
  parser. Hand-parsing pages, frames, varints, or
  cell records eats minutes and misses subtleties
  the format's runtime handles. The faster path,
  step by step: (a) copy the file and any
  sidecars to a working location; (b) examine the
  bytes — if they look random when they should
  have structure, the file is encrypted; (c) search
  the surrounding files for a key or transform
  (a small `.key` file, an environment variable
  named in a config, a comment in a schema or
  README, a constant value visible in repeating
  high-entropy bytes); (d) decrypt or decode the
  bytes and write the result back over the
  encrypted file in the working copy; (e) open the
  working copy through the format's normal client
  and let the runtime do the parsing and any
  pending-state recovery.
- **A journal contains UPDATEs as well as INSERTs.**
  A recovery that emits only the new rows added by
  the journal but keeps the original values for
  rows that the journal updated misses half the
  point. After the runtime applies the journal,
  query the merged state — rows whose values
  changed in the journal must show the journal's
  value, not the original. If the result looks
  like just the base file plus a few extra rows,
  the runtime didn't apply the journal or the
  recovery emitted from the pre-merge file.
- When the file's first bytes are a recognized
  magic number (gzip, zip, png, jpeg, etc.),
  decompress / decode through the standard library
  before parsing the inner data.

## Working with scripts that bring up services

A setup script that finishes leaving its services
running is the artifact; a script that finishes
with services not running, or that doesn't finish
at all, doesn't satisfy the contract.

- **Validate config before starting.** A daemon's
  own check flag (most have one — e.g. `<daemon> -t`
  for many web servers, `<daemon> -t -f <conf>` for
  others) catches syntax errors that would
  otherwise produce a non-starting daemon and a
  silent failure cascade. Run the check immediately
  after writing each config file, not just before
  the start line; exit on failure with the
  daemon's stderr visible so the line number and
  unexpected token are recoverable from the script
  output.
- **Config directives that include variable
  references usually need the value enclosed in
  quotes.** Web-server log-format directives are a
  common example: a line like
  `log_format <name> $variable1 $variable2;` is a
  syntax error because the parser sees the bare
  `$` as an unexpected token. The directive needs
  the format string in single or double quotes:
  `log_format <name> '$variable1 $variable2';`.
  Same rule applies to any directive value
  containing whitespace, dollar signs, semicolons,
  or other characters the directive parser treats
  as structural. When in doubt, quote the value.
- **Within a quoted format string, individual
  variables may also need their own embedded
  quotes** when the consumer of the resulting
  output (often a regex check on a log line)
  expects the value to appear quoted. For example,
  a check that looks for a trailing quoted token
  in a log line is satisfied only if the format
  string embeds the variable with surrounding
  quote characters in the format itself —
  `'$a $b $c "$d"'` produces a log line ending in
  `"<value of d>"`, whereas `'$a $b $c $d'` ends
  in a bare token. Match the shape the consumer
  expects.
- **Many config directives have scope requirements:
  the directive is only valid inside a specific
  block.** A daemon error like
  `"<directive>" directive is not allowed here in
  <file>:<line>` means the directive is in the
  wrong nesting level — it's inside an inner block
  (e.g. `server { ... }`) but the directive is only
  valid in an outer block (e.g. `http { ... }`).
  Move the directive to the outer block.

  Concrete patterns to remember for the
  web-server family:
    - Directives that *define* named configuration
      objects (log formats, rate-limit zones,
      upstream pools, shared memory zones,
      proxy caches) live in the outer block
      (`http { ... }`), not inside a per-site
      `server { ... }`.
    - Directives that *reference* those names
      (access_log <name>, limit_req zone=<name>,
      proxy_pass <pool>) go inside the `server` or
      `location` block where they apply.
    - When a configuration file is included from
      inside an outer block (e.g. a file in
      `/etc/nginx/conf.d/` is included from
      `http { }`), content at the FILE's top level
      is at http-level — so define-style
      directives can sit at the top of the file,
      BEFORE the `server { }` block, in the same
      file.
    - A definition must be parsed before the
      reference. Includes are processed in file-
      name order; a referencing block in an
      earlier-named file fails with "unknown name"
      if the defining directive is in a later-
      named file.
- **Invoke the daemon binary directly, not through
  an init-system wrapper.** `service` and
  `systemctl` are no-ops in environments without
  an init system; they return success without
  starting anything. The binary itself self-
  daemonizes in most cases (web servers, ssh
  daemons, database servers).
- **Confirm the service is listening before the
  script returns.** A bounded poll of the
  listening port — opening a TCP socket through
  bash's built-in pseudo-device or Python's
  `socket.create_connection` — works in any
  environment. Tools like `nc` are frequently
  missing from stripped containers; a loop whose
  probe always fails silently declares the service
  ready while it's still starting.
- **Don't let strict-mode error handling swallow
  an unstartable daemon.** A start command that
  prints nothing on failure produces a script that
  exits with success but with no service running.
  Wrap the invocation so a failure surfaces the
  daemon's error log before exiting.
- **Generate dependencies that the daemon
  requires.** Daemons that need host keys, system
  users, working directories, log files, or
  certificates require those to exist; generate or
  create them before the start line.
- **Setup scripts are checklists, not narratives.**
  Every component the spec requires must be:
  created, owned by the right user, permissioned
  correctly, configured to the named values,
  exposed at the named port, and running. A
  missing line — a `useradd`, a `chmod +x`, a
  `chown`, a service start, a port poll — breaks
  the dependency chain and collapses everything
  downstream of it.
- **A hook that must write to a directory another
  service owns needs write permission on that
  directory.** A push-receive deploy that copies
  files from a bare repo into a web server's
  document root requires the document root to be
  writable by the user the hook runs as (often
  the same user the bare repo is owned by).
  Without this, the hook silently fails or runs
  partially and the web server keeps serving the
  old content (or a 404). Make the deploy
  destination owned by, or group-writable to, the
  user the hook runs as. The end-to-end
  verification — clone, commit, push, then
  request the deployed URL — surfaces this
  immediately: if the response is the old content
  or a 404, the hook didn't deploy.
- **A refactor must preserve every action the
  original did.** Replacing one approach with
  another (one credential mechanism with another,
  one config-write style with another) frequently
  drops a step the replacement doesn't perform on
  its own. Read the full diff before saving:
  every check that currently passes must still
  pass.
- **Portable shell over installed tools.** A
  script that depends on a package that may not
  be present in a stripped environment fails
  silently or unpredictably. Prefer bash
  builtins, POSIX utilities, and standard-library
  Python over installed packages whenever the
  task allows.
- **Run the script yourself in the current shell
  before declaring it complete.** Check the exit
  code, then probe the services it was supposed
  to start (open a TCP socket to the documented
  port, make an HTTP request, look at the
  generated log line). If the exit code is
  non-zero, the script aborted early — find the
  failing command in the output and fix it. If
  the exit code is zero but services aren't
  responding, the script's start-up logic has a
  bug even though its overall control flow is
  clean.
- **A non-zero exit early in the script leaves
  every later service unstarted.** If the script
  is structured as a sequence of
  `<step> || exit 1` guards, the FIRST failing
  step aborts everything downstream. A config
  validation that fails on the web-server step
  takes down the SSH-start line that follows it,
  and every test depending on either service
  fails. Either validate all configs up front
  before any start lines, or arrange the script
  so independent services don't share an early-
  exit fate.

## Working with concurrent or asynchronous code

- **Each unit of work should be addressable.** When
  multiple tasks run together with bounded
  concurrency, hold a handle to each task that
  was actually started, so the unit can be
  signaled, cancelled, or awaited individually.
  Tasks queued behind a semaphore are not yet
  running; they have no cleanup to do.
- **Cancellation must reach what was running.** On
  an interrupt at the top level, walk the list of
  running task handles and signal each one
  explicitly, then wait for each one's cleanup
  path to complete. A gather that drops to the
  top without first signaling its children leaves
  cleanup blocks unexecuted.
- **Use the runtime's signal-handling integration
  rather than the OS's default.** Most async
  runtimes have a hook that translates OS signals
  into the runtime's own cancellation primitive,
  so the cancellation walks through `finally`
  blocks instead of killing the process between
  them.
- **Use a monotonic clock for elapsed-time
  reasoning.** Wall-clock time can jump.
- **Containers that grow with new entries need an
  independent shrink path.** Don't piggyback the
  cleanup on the same code path as the insertion;
  the cleanup must run on its own schedule.

## Iteration and saving

- **A working baseline saved on disk beats a
  better version still in progress.** When a task
  has a finite budget and a kill at the end of
  that budget, the file on disk at kill-time wins.
  Save the simplest version that satisfies the
  shape of the contract first; only then refine.
- **Refinement attempts should never overwrite a
  working baseline with an in-progress rewrite.**
  If the budget runs out mid-rewrite, the
  baseline you used to have is gone. Either write
  the refinement to a side path, exercise it, and
  swap it in only after it works; or accept that
  the baseline is your floor and refine only
  small areas at a time.
- **Cap structural refinement at three rounds.**
  If three rounds of changing the shape of the
  solution haven't moved the failing signal, the
  shape is wrong, not the parameters. Switch
  decomposition entirely or accept the partial
  result.
- **For approximating a reference output, keep the
  generator simple and fast.** When the task caps
  source size and the threshold is a similarity
  ratio against a reference, multi-bounce sampling
  approaches exceed wall-clock budgets long before
  converging. Closed-form per-pixel or per-cell
  evaluation — sample the reference at corners,
  edges, region centers; identify the dominant
  layers (background gradient, foreground shapes,
  lighting); encode each layer as an analytic
  expression — is faster, smaller, and tunable in
  a few iterations.
- **A size budget is a hard constraint, not an
  aspiration.** When a task caps source size
  (often gzipped, often a single-digit kilobyte
  limit like 2 KB), a submission that exceeds the
  cap fails the build / compile gate before any
  quality is measured — even if the code would
  otherwise work perfectly. Measure compressed
  size after each meaningful change
  (`gzip -c <file> | wc -c`); aim well under the
  cap (50% margin); favour terser expressions
  over elaborate logic; eliminate helpers that
  inline to fewer characters; shorten variable
  names once the algorithm is settled. A working
  submission at 80% of the cap beats a polished
  one at 800% of the cap, every time.
- **Don't exit early if no baseline is saved yet.**
  The protective heuristic — stop before a kill
  destroys progress — only applies once there's
  progress to protect.

## Tools available here

Shell, Python interpreter, file read/write — used
directly. Speculative imports of agent helper
packages that aren't installed raise import errors
and waste turns. Standard library and what's
already on the system only.

## Investigating an unfamiliar program or filter

Cheap inspection before expensive: list the working
directory, look at file bytes and printable
strings, ask for help / usage flags, run with the
simplest input and observe stdout, stderr, exit
code.

When one component processes data that another
component will execute or render, the gap between
how each parses the same bytes is where unexpected
behavior lives. Read the source of each side
before constructing candidate inputs. Look for
asymmetries in: how many passes a transformer
makes (single-pass strippers often leave residue
that reassembles into the thing they tried to
remove); how nested elements get treated
(recursion vs flat-walk); how namespace boundaries
shift parsing rules; how malformed delimiters get
resolved; how attribute encodings get decoded
relative to outer parsing layers.

The most reliable approach against a single-pass
stripping transformer is to nest a complete
instance of the dangerous token inside an outer
fragment of the same token's letters: the inner
instance is what the stripper removes; the outer
fragments fuse together into a fresh instance of
the same token that survives. Pick the split
position by reading the post-transform output and
confirming a clean, well-formed instance of the
token appears in the surviving text. If the
transformer instead runs to a fixed point
(repeating its strip until nothing changes), this
class doesn't apply; switch to looking for
parser-rule mismatches between the two layers.

Iterate from observation rather than theory:
construct a candidate, run it through the
transformer, inspect what comes out. Many inputs
that seem promising from prior knowledge are
blocked by current renderers — URL schemes that
used to be executable in attribute contexts no
longer fire, event-handler attributes that start
with a recognizable prefix are routinely stripped
by filters that do nothing else. The surviving
input needs to be something the renderer
executes on its own, not something requiring user
gesture or a renderer no longer in common use.

When a program processes user input by passing it
to a function whose first argument is meant to be
a format string (a printf-family call where the
input IS the format, not just an argument to a
format), supplying format-specifier characters as
input causes the function to print adjacent memory.
Simple specifier sequences probe what gets leaked.
When a program refuses to run under inspection
(anti-debug guard), the guard is usually a short
call near program start; the program's data and
code can often be read directly without running it.

## Before stopping

Read the artifact on disk. If it doesn't match the
latest thinking, update it once more.
